abstract: Indirect prompt-injection (IPI) benchmarks predominantly test planted instructions that redirect a tool-using agent toward an attacker-chosen task. Yet attacker-controlled content can instead tamper with the outcome of the task already in progress. For example, a buyer’s dispute evidence can cite a false refund policy to inflate the refund without redirecting the agent away from resolving the dispute. We define IPI by authority rather than instruction-like wording: planted content constitutes an attack when it attempts to influence a decision that its source is not authorized to determine. We introduce a benchmark that makes this boundary explicit: in each of 90 validated cases across three tool-use environments, the user request specifies the source that resolves the targeted decision. Every attack tampers with a decision required by the benign task rather than replacing that task. Each case has attacks with the same harmful outcome that target up to six parts of the agent’s decision making: its objective, decision rules, available actions, expected consequences, reading of observations, or beliefs about the current state. Without a defense, attacks on three of the five other targets (decision rules, available actions, and state) have higher mean success than objective attacks across five LLMs. A detection-and-removal defense reduces objective-targeting attacks to 2.4% success but leaves observation- and state-targeting attacks at 9.5% and 12.1%; this gap persists under detection-optimized rewrites. A tool-policy defense still allows 15.4% attack success, close to 17.0% without a defense, because these attacks generally retain expected tools and manipulate values obtained during execution. Evaluations whose attacks redirect the task or target only the agent’s objective can therefore overestimate the coverage of these defenses. Code and data are available at https://github.com/amazon-science/task-tampering-prompt-injection.

sections.body: The section argues that **indirect prompt injection** should be defined by authority: external content is an attack when it tries to influence a decision its source is not authorized to determine. Instruction-like wording alone does not mark an attack, and a false claim from an authorized source is misinformation rather than injection. The authors say existing defenses may miss such tampering. Detectors can lose the instruction or off-task signals they rely on, and plan or policy checks can pass a tampered call that uses an expected tool. The paper introduces 90 validated cases across productivity, DevOps, and marketplace environments, each with a compound attack and single-primitive attacks for up to six primitives.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Existing injection benchmarks mostly test instructions that redirect agents, so tampering with in-progress decisions goes untested.

sections.body: The section groups related work by mechanism. Most benchmarks evaluate attacker-written instructions that redirect the agent, and most defenses target that form. Prompting and training defenses shape how the model treats external data but do not constrain the calls it emits. Detection defenses classify or remove suspected injections, so their coverage depends on the content being recognizable. Plan- and policy-based defenses check calls against a tool set, policy, or plan, and generally do not constrain free-text arguments. Architectural and information-flow systems enforce source or flow policies but do not establish the truth or topic-specific authority of admitted content. Evidence and authorization defenses still rely on judging benign content or on an authorization graph derived from the request.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior benchmarks and defenses mostly assume instruction-bearing attacks, and each defense family limits a different kind of influence.

sections.body: The threat model treats the attacker as a legitimate environment participant, such as a vendor, buyer, or repository contributor, who can write only to sources normally controlled by that role. The attacker cannot change the system prompt, observe reasoning, intercept tool calls, or alter others' data, and does not know the user's exact task. The attack goal is task tampering: a harmful deviation in a decision that tasks consulting the source foreseeably involve. The section gives three conditions for a case to count as indirect prompt injection: the attacker controls content the agent encounters, the user request designates the source that resolves the targeted decision, and accepting the content produces a predefined harmful outcome. In the inflated-refund example, the buyer claims a refund of 1,074.99 USD while the platform record authorizes 899.99 USD.
sections.heading: Threat Model
sections.headline: The attacker plants content in a role-appropriate source and can tamper with a decision the task consults that source for.

sections.body: The benchmark co-designs the benign task, attacker role, controlled source, targeted decision, resolution basis, and harmful outcome for each case, within rules for each environment's personas and knowledge. Table 1 lists 90 retained cases, 52 with structured effects and 38 with free-form effects, and 1,343 single-primitive attacks. Two annotators reviewed 111 designed cases, with agreement of 91.9% overall. Human annotation of attacks agreed with the assigned primitive in 96.4% of cases. Automatic scores agreed with human annotation in 97.2% of task and attack judgments. Each case keeps one benign task and one harmful outcome, and only the planted content varies across six primitives: objective, decision rule, consequence model, action space, observation interpretation, and world state.
sections.heading: Benchmark
sections.headline: The benchmark has 90 retained cases with 1,343 single-primitive attacks across productivity, DevOps, and marketplace environments.

sections.body: The experiments run five models (DeepSeek V3.1, Kimi K2.5, Claude Sonnet 4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, GLM-5) as ReAct agents at temperature 0 against seven defenses from five mechanism families. Without a defense, mean attack success across models is 17.0 percent overall. By primitive, objective attacks reach 15.0, decision-rule attacks 21.2, consequence attacks 13.7, action-space attacks 19.0, observation attacks 12.4, and state attacks 18.6. Benign task success without an injection is 95.3 percent. Table 3 reports these as percentages. Appendix G gives uncertainty estimates that resample cases rather than runs, and each configuration is run once.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Without a defense, decision-rule, action, and state attacks succeed more often than objective attacks, across five models.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the definition: planted content is an attack when it tries to influence a decision its source is not authorized to determine, even when it only tampers with the task in progress. Objective attacks, which prior evaluations mainly test, already succeed less often without a defense than attacks on decision rules, actions, and state. Objective attacks also remain among the three lowest-success primitives under every defense except CaMeL. The paper proposes two design directions: screening that asks whether a source is authorized to determine the targeted decision, and action checks that admit each consequential argument only from an authorized source. These are presented as directions for design.
sections.heading: Discussion and Conclusion
sections.headline: Defenses tested mainly on redirecting instructions leave task tampering partly uncovered, so screening should also check source authority.

sections.body: The appendix covers benchmark construction, including 28 checks under 20 principles and the 18 attack categories of Table 5. It describes three environments with 25 tools and 91 actions. It then gives the scoring method: boolean checks over tool calls, with an LLM judge run three times on extracted free-form fields and a predicate that holds on two of three YES votes. It reports human validation, a complete example case, the trust-hierarchy prompts, the annotation protocol, uncertainty estimates, and run configuration. The limitations cover scale, the simulated domains, a single-shot attacker that does not adapt to defenses, the defense adaptations, and the use of Claude models both to draft cases and as evaluated agents.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists construction stages, 18 attack categories, environment tools, scoring and validation checks, models, and limitations.
